name: Bank conversion + SWIFT wire — Bank of China
status_note: Lawful where the RMB is documented current-account income; the bank must accept the source-of-funds file.
summary: Sell RMB for USD on the bank's published board and send a telegraphic transfer to your own U.S. account. This is the reference route: fully published price, published fee formula, published statutory basis.
steps: Confirm which rulebook you fall under: a foreign national continuously resident in China for one year or more is a 'domestic individual' under Art. 52(2) of Decree 532, while the conversion of a non-domestic individual's China income is governed by Huifa [2007] No. 1 Art. 13 and Huifa [2020] No. 14 Art. 59 (S07, S09, S10).

Assemble the source-of-funds file: passport, the bank card/account, employment contract or service agreement, payslips, and the China tax record (纳税记录 / 完税证明) covering the years the balance was earned (S10).

Ask the branch whether a tax recordal (税务备案) is required for the payment; a single outward payment of USD 50,000 or more for listed service-trade and income items is within Announcement [2013] No. 40 (S13).
Execute the FX sale at the counter or in the app; the trade rate is the bank's live selling rate, not the board snapshot used in these tables (S01).
Send the wire with the beneficiary name exactly matching your U.S. account. Keep the FX slip and the wire confirmation.
Report the account on FinCEN Form 114 if the aggregate exceeded USD 10,000 at any point in the year, and check Form 8938 thresholds (S20, S22).
pros: Published rate and published fee formula, so the cost is estimable before you commit.
No third-party intermediary, no counterparty risk beyond the banking system.
Statutory basis is explicit for documented current-account income.
Foreign tax credit and §988 treatment are ordinary, documented outcomes.
cons: Requires a complete, consistent paper trail; the bank can decline an incomplete file.
The fee is capped but the spread is not, so the real cost is the bank's markup on the day.
Correspondent-bank deductions are not published (F05).
A tax recordal step may be required at USD 50,000 and above (S13).

name: Bank conversion + SWIFT wire — China Merchants Bank
status_note: Same legal basis as M01; CMB's fee cap is higher and its published board is one day behind at retrieval.
summary: Same route through China Merchants Bank. Higher fee ceiling (CNY 1,000 versus CNY 260) but a competitive board.
steps: Same document set as M01 (S10).

Check whether the funding account holds RMB cash or RMB remittance funds: CMB charges 0.8% to convert USD cash into remittance funds, but nothing when the account already holds remittance funds (S04).
Choose the charging method deliberately: SHA (you pay your bank's fees), BEN (beneficiary pays) or OUR (you prepay the equivalent of USD 25 and may be asked for more) (S04).
Execute the sale, then the wire; keep the FX slip and the SWIFT confirmation.
Complete the U.S. reporting checks in M01.
pros: Published 0.1% fee with a stated cap and a stated cable charge.
Explicit SHA/BEN/OUR disclosure, which most banks do not publish.
Board readable without a browser session.
cons: Fee ceiling is CNY 1,000 — four times BOC's cap.
The OUR option can cost more than the published prepayment if the intermediary asks for more.
CMB's board carried the previous day's date at retrieval (F02).

name: HSBC China outward telegraphic transfer (Premier / Advance)
status_note: Lawful, but the Premier/Advance service tier and its eligibility must be held; the Board's latest tariff charges a wider spread than the mainland peers read here.
summary: HSBC China's published tariff and board, priced for a Premier/Advance customer. Fee is lower in the middle range than the peers; the spread is the widest of the three readable banks.
steps: Confirm the account tier and whether the monthly relationship-balance condition is met (S06).
Assemble the same source-of-funds file (S10).
Decide whether to buy 'Pay Exact': it adds CNY 200 so the beneficiary receives the full instructed amount (S06).
Execute the sale and the transfer; retain the tariff reference and the SWIFT confirmation.
Complete the U.S. reporting checks in M01.
pros: Published tariff effective 31 October 2026, including the cable charge.
Lowest published fee cap of the three readable banks (CNY 500).
Pay Exact makes the receiving amount deterministic for a fixed extra fee.
cons: Widest measured spread: about 0.47% versus a 6.6764 reference mid, roughly double BOC's.
Tier requirements mean the price is not available to everyone.
Pay Exact is an extra 0.2% at USD 10,000 and is not refundable if the transfer fails.

name: HSBC China outward transfer — individual Private Banking
status_note: The tariff shows zero for individual Private Banking customers on both the transfer and the cable line; eligibility and relationship-balance thresholds are not established in the excerpt read.
summary: Same HSBC board with the Private Banking tariff column: no transfer fee and no cable charge. Cost reduces to the spread alone.
steps: Establish whether the account qualifies for the individual Private Banking tariff (S06).
If it does, the enumerated steps are the same as M03 minus the fee lines.
If it does not, use M03 or M01 instead; do not assume the zero fee.
pros: No published transfer or cable fee for individual Private Banking customers.
Deterministic: the only cost left is the spread.
cons: Eligibility is not verified here and may require a large relationship balance (F08).
The spread is still the widest of the readable banks.
A zero fee does not make this cheaper than BOC at any tier modelled, because the spread dominates.

name: Foreign-currency cash carry (bank cash purchase + hand carry)
status_note: Lawful only within the cash-carry limits; unusable for a six-figure balance without repeated trips, each of which is separately regulated.
summary: Buy USD cash at the bank and carry it out. The published cost is only the spread, but the legal ceiling is USD 5,000 per trip without a permit and USD 10,000 with one.
steps: Buy USD cash at a bank; BOC's board shows the same selling price for cash and remittance on the date read (S01).
Up to USD 5,000 equivalent: no carrying permit needed (S16).
USD 5,000-10,000: obtain a 《携带外汇出境许可证》 from the bank; the bank may only issue up to the deposit or purchase amount (S16).
Above USD 10,000: in principle not permitted; only listed special cases can apply to SAFE (S16).
On arrival in the United States, file FinCEN Form 105 for more than USD 10,000 (S17).
Deposit the cash: U.S. banks may apply their own cash-deposit rules and ask for source documentation.
pros: No wire fee at all.
The bank's cash selling price matched its remittance selling price on the date read, so the spread cost is the same as M01.
Statutory limits are explicit and easy to check.
cons: Cannot move USD 400,000 this way: 40 permitted trips at USD 10,000 would each need a permit and a border crossing.
Physical loss, theft and seizure risk; CBP reporting is mandatory above USD 10,000.
Repeated same-day and short-interval trips are capped at USD 500 and USD 1,000 (S16).
Declared cash is visible to both customs authorities.

name: Wise (transfer from a China bank app or Alipay)
status_note: Available only to a non-mainland-Chinese customer who worked in China and holds a China tax record showing tax paid within the last three years.
published_caps: CNY 300,000 per transfer from a China bank app
Overall limit = salary earned in China minus tax paid in China
summary: Wise routes the payment through a PBOC-licensed partner and applies its own limit equal to after-tax salary. Its CNY fee is not published as a table, so no all-in figure is stated.
steps: Check the eligibility list on Wise's own help page: not mainland Chinese; has worked in China; valid China tax record showing tax paid in the last three years (S24).
Create the transfer and complete verification; Wise says this takes 1-2 working days the first time (S24).
The recipient must be an account you own outside China, or your Wise account (S24).
Observe the single-transfer caps: CNY 300,000 from the bank app, CNY 50,000 from Alipay (S24).
Keep the tax records: Wise may request new records when the limit is reached (S24).
Complete the U.S. reporting checks in M01.
pros: Publishes its eligibility rules and limits, so a reader can rule themselves in or out quickly.
Runs through a PBOC-licensed partner, so it is not an underground channel.
Handles the FX and the payment in one instruction.
cons: The fee and the applied rate are only shown inside the transfer flow, so no pre-computed all-in cost can be published (F07).
The limit is after-tax salary, which may be far below the account balance.
Only a non-mainland-Chinese customer qualifies, and only for an account the sender owns.
Tax records older than three years are not accepted.

name: Bank conversion + SWIFT wire — Agricultural Bank of China
status_note: Same legal basis as M01. The ABC board is script-rendered and returned no rate, so the row is published blank.
summary: A fourth state-owned bank on the same legal footing. No ABC rate could be read at retrieval, so no cost is asserted.
steps: The steps are those of M01.
Obtain the branch's current selling rate and fee schedule in writing before executing.
pros: Same statutory basis as M01.
A competing quote is useful leverage when comparing banks.
cons: No published rate readable at retrieval (the board is script-rendered), so nothing is costed.
No ABC fee table was read this pass.
A blank row is not evidence of a low or high price.

name: Bank conversion + SWIFT wire — ICBC
status_note: Same legal basis as M01. The ICBC board returned 'no data' to a text fetch.
summary: ICBC's board is populated by script after page load, and returned an empty table. No rate and no fee are asserted.
steps: The steps are those of M01.
Read the live counter rate and the bank's price list before committing.
pros: Same statutory basis as M01.
Largest branch network, which matters for in-person document review.
cons: Nothing priced: the board and the price list could not be read (S25, F04).
A branch quote is the only reliable input.

name: Bank conversion + SWIFT wire — China Construction Bank
status_note: Same legal basis as M01. The CCB quotation page did not return its table to a text fetch.
summary: CCB's quotation page is script-rendered; no rate was read, and no CCB fee table was located.
steps: The steps are those of M01.
Ask the branch for the fee schedule in writing.
pros: Same statutory basis as M01.
cons: No published rate readable at retrieval.
No fee schedule read, so the row is blank (F04).

name: Annual USD 50,000 quota purchase (domestic individual)
status_note: The quota is a documented annual aggregate for an individual's FX settlement and a domestic individual's FX purchase. Whether a U.S. citizen falls inside it depends on classification under Decree 532 Art. 52(2) and must be confirmed with the bank.
summary: The familiar USD 50,000 figure is an annual aggregate quota, not a tax and not a price. Priced here on BOC's tariff, it is the same bank route with a hard annual ceiling.
steps: Establish the classification first; the quota does not apply identically to a non-domestic individual (S07 Art. 52(2), S09 Art. 2, Art. 13).
Within the quota, present valid ID at the bank (S09 Art. 2).
Above the quota, a current-account payment proceeds on documents under Art. 12 or Art. 13, or a capital-account payment under the capital rules (S09).
Keep the bank's quota record: the quota is an annual aggregate per person, not per transaction.
Do not split a larger amount across people or days to stay under it (S08 Art. 7).
pros: Simple documentation inside the quota.
Same published bank pricing as M01.
cons: Caps at USD 50,000 per person per year, so it cannot clear a USD 400,000 balance in one year.
Applicability to a foreign national is a classification question, not a certainty (F12).
Using relatives' quotas to move your own money is the prohibited 'splitting into small batches' pattern (S08 Art. 7).

name: Emigration property transfer (SAFE-approved lump sum)
status_note: Requires emigration and SAFE approval at the branch where the original permanent residence was registered, with the ceiling set by the approval document.
summary: A one-off capital-account transfer of pre-emigration domestic assets, approved by SAFE and then remitted by the bank in one sum or in batches.
steps: Confirm the pre-emigration asset and emigration facts that the regime requires (S09 Art. 20, S11).
Apply to the SAFE branch in the place of the original registered permanent residence (S11).
Obtain the approval document, which sets the amount that may be remitted (S11).
Take the approval to the bank; it may remit in one lump sum or in several batches within that limit (S11).
Complete the U.S. reporting and §988 checks (S19, S20).
pros: Designed for exactly this fact pattern: a large lawful balance leaving after emigration.
The ceiling is set by an approval document rather than a generic annual quota.
Batching within one approval is expressly allowed.
cons: Requires the emigration facts and the correct SAFE branch; not a walk-in bank product.
The application document list is not restated here because the underlying property-transfer measures were not re-read (F10).
SAFE approval is discretionary and can take time.

name: Inheritance transfer of an estate's domestic assets
status_note: Requires an inheritance and SAFE approval at the branch of the decedent's pre-death residence; the notarisation requirement for property documents was removed in 2014.
summary: The inheritance counterpart of M11, including the 2014 change that allows one combined application where assets come from several decedents.
steps: Establish the inheritance documentation required by the property-transfer measures (S09 Art. 20).
Apply to the SAFE branch where the decedent's residence was registered before death (S11).
Where several decedents are involved, a combined application may be filed at one branch (S11).
Remit in one sum or in batches within the approval (S11).
Complete the U.S. reporting and §988 checks (S19, S20).
pros: Expressly contemplated by the rules, including multi-decedent estates.
Some notarisation steps were removed in 2014.
cons: Requires an estate and SAFE approval; not available for ordinary savings.
Document list not restated here (F10).

name: Property-sale proceeds remittance (with tax-clearance certificate)
status_note: Requires SAFE review of the purchase-FX application, the transfer contract and the property-transfer tax-clearance certificate.
summary: If the balance is the proceeds of a mainland property sale, the route is a SAFE-reviewed conversion supported by the tax-clearance certificate for the transfer.
steps: Obtain the property-transfer tax-clearance certificate (完税证明) (S12).
Assemble the FX purchase application and the transfer contract (S12).
Submit to the SAFE branch where the property is located for review (S12).
Convert and remit through the bank on approval.
Complete the U.S. reporting and §988 checks (S19, S20).
pros: A defined route with a published document list.
The tax-clearance certificate doubles as evidence of the source of funds.
cons: If the sale has not been taxed correctly, the route stops at the certificate.
Review is by SAFE, not only the bank.

name: Entrusted conversion by a direct relative
status_note: Permitted for quota-level settlement and purchase by a direct relative (parent, child, spouse) with identity, authorisation and relationship documents; above the quota the documents behind the transaction are also required.
summary: The rules do allow a direct relative to handle a quota-level conversion for you. They do not allow a crowd of friends to each use their quota for your money.
steps: Confirm the relationship is within the definition: parent, child or spouse (S09 Art. 38).
Provide both parties' ID, your written authorisation and the relationship document (S09 Art. 38).
Handle the conversion within the annual quota; above it, add the transaction documents (S09 Art. 4, Art. 12).
Do not extend the arrangement to non-relatives or repeat it to defeat the quota (S08 Art. 7).
pros: Explicitly permitted for direct relatives.
Useful where the account holder cannot attend a branch.
cons: Limited to parent, child or spouse — not friends, not cousins.
Still capped by the quota.
Easy to drift into the prohibited splitting pattern if repeated.

name: Offshore RMB (CNH) transfer to a Hong Kong account, then convert
status_note: A cross-border RMB current-account remittance to an account you hold offshore is contemplated by the rules, but no bank read this pass publishes the fee for it.
summary: Send RMB rather than USD, then convert offshore. The appeal is avoiding the onshore USD purchase; the problem is that no published fee was found and the offshore spread is a second cost.
steps: Establish that the payment qualifies as a current-account cross-border RMB remittance and that the receiving bank accepts it.
Obtain the sending and receiving banks' fee schedules and the applicable CNH spread in writing.
Only then compare the all-in number with M01.
pros: Two spreads do not necessarily cost more than one if the offshore market is tighter.
Keeps the onshore conversion out of the picture entirely.
cons: No published fee found in this pass, so no cost is asserted (F15).
Requires an offshore account you already hold or can open.
Two sets of bank compliance, two sets of documents.

name: Card spending and ATM withdrawal abroad (UnionPay)
status_note: A lawful way to spend or withdraw modest amounts abroad, but the annual withdrawal caps were not re-verified from an official page this pass.
summary: Spend the RMB directly abroad. Useful for consumption, unusable as a way to repatriate a balance, and the caps are not re-verified here.
steps: Confirm the card's overseas cash-withdrawal cap and fee with the issuing bank.
Confirm the daily withdrawal limit and whether the card is enabled for the destination.
Treat any use as consumption, not as a transfer of capital.
pros: No formal outward-remittance paperwork.
Spends the balance at the card's conversion rate.
cons: Not a mechanism for moving a six-figure balance.
Caps and fees not re-verified this pass (F14).
Leaves no clean audit trail for a large capital movement.

name: Crypto / USDT over-the-counter conversion
status_note: Converting between legal tender and virtual currency inside China is prohibited as illegal financial activity; no instructions are given.
summary: Listed because it is the route most often suggested online. It is prohibited in China, and the statutory penalty attaches to the amount moved.
steps: No execution steps are provided. The route is prohibited under Yinfa [2026] No. 42 (S15), which repealed the 2021 notice.
pros: None that survive contact with the rules: the activity is characterised as illegal financial activity in China.
cons: Illegal financial activity under Yinfa [2026] No. 42 (S15).
Penalty exposure under the FX Regulations for illegal FX trading: up to 30% of the amount, or 30% to an equal amount if serious (S07 Art. 45).
Counterparty and seizure risk, and a U.S. tax basis problem on top.

name: Underground bank / mirrored swap (对敲)
status_note: Private and disguised trading of foreign exchange is an enforcement target with statutory penalties.
summary: An offshore counterparty pays you dollars and is paid RMB inside China. Prohibited, and the penalty is proportional to the amount.
steps: No execution steps are provided. See Art. 45 of Decree 532 (S07).
pros: None lawful.
cons: Falls within 'private or disguised trading of foreign exchange' (S07 Art. 45): up to 30% of the amount, or 30% to an equal amount if serious.
Counterparty default risk with no legal recourse.
The U.S. side still has to be reported and taxed.

name: Quota splitting across family and friends (蚂蚁搬家)
status_note: Splitting a large amount into small batches to evade limit administration is expressly prohibited.
summary: Twenty friends each use their USD 50,000 quota. This is the specific behaviour the rules name and prohibit.
steps: No execution steps are provided. See Art. 7 of PBOC Decree [2006] No. 3 (S08).
pros: None lawful.
cons: Expressly prohibited as evasion of limit administration (S08 Art. 7).
Penalty exposure under Art. 40 or Art. 48 of Decree 532 for illegal arbitrage or false documents (S07).
Puts each relative's own FX record at risk.

name: Fabricated trade or service invoices
status_note: Using false or invalid transaction documents to buy foreign exchange is illegal arbitrage.
summary: Manufacturing a contract or invoice to justify a purchase. Prohibited, and it also creates a false U.S. tax position.
steps: No execution steps are provided. See Art. 40 of Decree 532 (S07) and Art. 7 of Decree [2006] No. 3 (S08).
pros: None lawful.
cons: Illegal arbitrage under Art. 40: fine up to 30%, or 30% to an equal amount if serious (S07).
Art. 48 separately penalises false documents (up to CNY 50,000 for an individual).
A fabricated paper trail contaminates the U.S. return as well.

name: Greater Bay Area Wealth Management Connect
status_note: A closed-loop investment channel for eligible GBA residents; the money stays inside the scheme and cannot be used to repatriate a balance.
summary: Listed to close the gap: it is a real cross-boundary scheme, but it is closed-loop and residence-restricted, so it is not a repatriation route.
steps: None applicable to a U.S. citizen repatriating a mainland balance.
pros: A lawful cross-boundary scheme for those it is designed for.
cons: Closed-loop by design.
Residence-restricted to the Greater Bay Area.
Not a way to get a balance out.

name: QDII funds and Stock Connect
status_note: Investment channels that convert RMB into foreign assets inside a quota; they do not deliver cash to a U.S. account.
summary: You can invest offshore through approved institutions, but the money is invested, not repatriated, and selling brings it back onshore.
steps: Not a repatriation route; no steps given.
pros: Diversification inside the rules.
cons: Does not put dollars in a U.S. bank account.
Carries market risk on top of the FX question.

name: Offshore payroll by the China employer
status_note: Solves future salary flows, not an existing balance already sitting in a mainland account.
summary: Ask the employer to pay part of future salary offshore. It does not move the balance that already exists.
steps: Not applicable to a balance already held; no steps given.
pros: Avoids the onshore conversion for future income.
cons: Does nothing for the existing balance.
Employer and PRC payroll-tax consequences are not assessed here.

name: Borrow offshore against the RMB deposit
status_note: No official mechanism was located in this pass by which a mainland RMB deposit can collateralise a U.S. dollar loan abroad.
summary: Sometimes proposed as 'don't convert, borrow'. No official route was found; cross-border guarantees are separately regulated and require approval.
steps: No verified steps. Cross-border guarantees require SAFE approval under Art. 19 of Decree 532 (S07).
pros: Would defer the conversion if it existed.
cons: No mechanism located (F15).
Cross-border security and guarantees are separately regulated.
Adds interest cost to the FX cost.
